##### **1.5 Motion Under Constant Acceleration: Direct and Integral Formulations**

When the acceleration of a particle is invariant over time, the motion is termed **uniformly accelerated motion**. Under the condition $a(t) = a = \text{const}$, the instantaneous acceleration coincides identically with the **average acceleration** across any arbitrary duration $t$:

$$a = a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v - v_0}{t - 0}$$

where $v_0$ is the **initial velocity** at time $t = 0$, and $v$ is the velocity at time $t$. Rearranging this algebraic definition directly produces the linear velocity relation:

$$v(t) = v_0 + at$$

In calculus formulation, instantaneous acceleration is defined by $a = dv/dt$. Separating variables gives the differential relation $dv = a(t)\,dt$. Integrating both sides from the initial state $(t = 0, v = v_i)$ to an arbitrary evaluation time $(t = T, v = v(T))$ yields the general first integral:

$$v(T) = v_i + \int_0^T a(t)\,dt$$

Because $a$ is constant, it factors out of the integrand, reducing the integral to $a \int_0^T dt = aT$:

$$v(T) = v_i + aT \implies v(t) = v_0 + at$$

Reconstructing the position requires a second integration of the velocity definition $v = dx/dt$. For a particle starting at **initial position** $x_i$ at $t = 0$, the exact position at time $T$ is given by the integral of $v(t)$:

$$x(T) = x_i + \int_0^T v(t)\,dt$$

Substituting the integral form of $v(t)$ into the trajectory equation yields a nested double integral:

$$x(T) = x_i + \int_0^T \left(v_i + \int_0^t a(h)\,dh\right) dt = x_i + v_i T + \int_0^T dt \int_0^t a(h)\,dh$$

where $h$ is a dummy variable of integration for the inner acceleration integral. For a constant acceleration $a(h) = a$, the inner integral evaluates to $at$:

$$\int_0^T dt \int_0^t a\,dh = \int_0^T at\,dt = a \left[ \frac{t^2}{2} \right]_0^T = \frac{1}{2}aT^2$$

Substituting this result yields the canonical quadratic equation of motion:

$$x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$

For unidirectional rectilinear motion where the velocity does not change sign ($v(t) \ge 0$), the total distance covered or **path length** $S$ equals the displacement and is computed directly from the velocity integral:

$$S = \int v(t)\,dt$$

Pursuit problems frequently feature delayed activation where an intercepting vehicle accelerates from rest after an elapsed latency. Consider a motorist passing a stationary police motorcycle at constant speed $v_c = 31\text{ m/s}$. The officer remains at rest for a reaction latency $\Delta t_d = 2.5\text{ s}$, then accelerates in pursuit at constant acceleration $a_m = 3.6\text{ m/s}^2$. 

Setting the coordinate origin $x = 0$ at the initial station of the officer and $t = 0$ at the instant the motorist passes, the motion of the car is uniform:

$$x_c(t) = v_c t = 31 t$$

The motorcycle remains at the origin until $t = \Delta t_d$. For all times $t \ge \Delta t_d$, its elapsed acceleration time is $t - \Delta t_d$, with initial velocity $v_{m0} = 0$:

$$x_m(t) = \frac{1}{2} a_m (t - \Delta t_d)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3.6)(t - 2.5)^2 = 1.8(t - 2.5)^2$$

Overtake occurs at the instant $t^*$ when the positions coincide, $x_c(t^*) = x_m(t^*)$:

$$31 t^* = 1.8 \left( (t^*)^2 - 5 t^* + 6.25 \right) = 1.8 (t^*)^2 - 9 t^* + 11.25$$

Grouped into standard quadratic form:

$$1.8 (t^*)^2 - 40 t^* + 11.25 = 0$$

Applying the quadratic formula:

$$t^* = \frac{40 \pm \sqrt{40^2 - 4(1.8)(11.25)}}{2(1.8)} = \frac{40 \pm \sqrt{1600 - 81}}{3.6} = \frac{40 \pm \sqrt{1519}}{3.6}$$

Evaluating $\sqrt{1519} \approx 38.974$ s yields the physical root satisfying $t^* > \Delta t_d$:

$$t^* = \frac{40 + 38.974}{3.6} \approx 21.94\text{ s}$$

The position of intercept is:

$$x^* = x_c(t^*) = 31 \times 21.94 \approx 680.1\text{ m}$$

The speed of the officer at the moment of overtake is determined by the linear velocity law evaluated over the acceleration interval $t^* - \Delta t_d$:

$$v_m(t^*) = a_m (t^* - \Delta t_d) = 3.6 \times (21.94 - 2.5) = 3.6 \times 19.44 \approx 70.0\text{ m/s}$$
